entry.title: Security analysis of the cubic UOV variant CML
entry.summary: On the Security of the Cubic UOV Variant CML IACR ePrint · Nov 12, 2026This paper analyzes CML, a cubic multivariate signature scheme over F_{2^8} designed to hide cubic term positions. The authors show that the cubic homogeneous parts of the public key span a space of dimension at most two, which leads to a procedure for recovering an equivalent key. Their implementation recovered an equivalent key in under 5 minutes for each tested parameter set, including the set targeting 256-bit security.

entry.title: Optimized Strategy and Two-Step Estimator for Solving LWE with Side-Channel Hints
entry.summary: Optimized Solving Strategy and Two-Step Estimator for LWE with Hints IACR ePrint · Nov 12, 2026Side-channel hints can lower the cost of solving the Learning with Errors (LWE) problem. The paper optimizes a two-step approach that applies BKZ reduction followed by final lattice sieving, jointly choosing block sizes, tour counts, and the sieving configuration. It also introduces a two-step estimator that predicts the reduced-basis profile and the probability of secret recovery. Experiments show the strategy significantly outperforms prior methods by Cao et al. and May and Nowakowski.

entry.title: Triads Below the ISA: Optimizing Cryptographic Software in CPU Microcode
entry.summary: Triads below the ISA: Optimizing Cryptographic Software in CPU Microcode IACR ePrint · Nov 12, 2026This paper treats the programmable microcode layer of x86 processors as a distinct target architecture for cryptographic computation and tailors implementations to its state, operations, invocation interface, capacity, and scheduling resources. The authors apply this method on Intel Goldmont to Keccak-f[1600] and X25519. Their Keccak implementation cuts permutation latency by 7.36% versus the fastest native implementation compared. The complete X25519 implementation needs 7.3% fewer cycles than s2n-bignum and 9.8% fewer than OpenSSL.

entry.title: Security analysis of anonymous authentication in Apple's Private Cloud Compute
entry.summary: Security Analysis of Anonymous Authentication in Apple's Private Cloud Compute IACR ePrint · Nov 12, 2026This paper examines the custom authentication protocol behind Apple's Private Cloud Compute, which sends on-device tasks such as language-model prompts to the cloud. The authors formalize the goals such a protocol needs, including rate limiting, user anonymity, and accountability, under the name PORTA. They analyze Apple's protocol against these properties. They also propose an alternative based on anonymous credentials, which they state achieves all of them.

entry.title: Encrypted authorship matching for fraud investigations
entry.summary: Encrypted Authorship Attribution for Fraud Detection IACR ePrint · Nov 12, 2026Authorship attribution links anonymous or disputed texts to known writers based on their writing style, which can help investigate phishing, impersonation, and investment scams. This paper studies privacy-preserving stylometric attribution using fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), focusing on Burrows' Delta, a method based on token frequency statistics and z-score comparisons. The authors present a homomorphic implementation and show with the CKKS scheme that the full pipeline runs without bootstrapping while maintaining high numerical accuracy.

entry.title: Testing whether models that secretly underperform can evade detection
entry.summary: Stress-Testing Sandbagging Detection Under Adaptive Attack arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper examines sandbagging, where a model deliberately scores low on evaluations while keeping its underlying capability, and whether detectors can catch it. The authors fine-tune small open-weight models to fail GSM8K math problems only when an audit marker appears, then adapt the attack over two retraining rounds against a text-based audit. After retraining, the audit's AUC fell from 0.978 to 0.560, and it missed nearly all retrained models. The authors conclude that a detector catching a fixed attack does not show it will catch an adaptive one.

entry.title: Keeping the Flaw, Silencing the Alert: Testing CodeQL Taint Tracking with Natural Rewrites
entry.summary: Preserve the Vulnerability, Break the Alert: Testing the Robustness of CodeQL Taint Tracking with Natural Rewrites arXiv · Nov 13, 2026The paper tests how robust CodeQL's JavaScript taint tracking is to natural rewrites that keep a vulnerability intact. A large language model, without knowing the analyzer's internals, rewrote one function on each reported flow, and the flaw survived while the alert disappeared for 26.2% of 172 real npm flows. All silencing rewrites trace to seven gaps at the library-modeling boundary, and many also fool other taint analyzers. The authors conclude that a vanished alert is weak evidence that a vulnerability has been fixed. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors test CodeQL taint tracking with vulnerability-preserving rewrites on 172 real npm flows, silencing 26.2%, traced to seven library-modeling gaps and cross-checked on other analyzers.

entry.title: CapLite: Blocking prompt injection in small AI agents without trusting model-written security rules
entry.summary: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper studies defenses against prompt injection, where malicious text tricks an AI agent into harmful actions. Existing enforcement methods ask the agent's own model to write security policies that code then enforces, and the authors find that small models often write flawed policies. They propose CapLite, which derives its policy from tool schemas and only allows write actions whose target details appear in the user's request. In 13,935 attacked AgentDojo episodes, no attack succeeded, with utility under attack comparable to CaMeL at much lower token cost.

entry.title: A paper on cryptographically non-linear all-or-nothing transforms, cryptographic building blocks that hide all input data unless the full output is known.
entry.summary: On cryptographically non-linear all-or-nothing transforms arXiv · Nov 13, 2026The paper studies unconditionally secure all-or-nothing transforms (AONTs) that are cryptographically non-linear. It enumerates small (t,3,3) AONTs computationally and shows that non-additive AONTs exist. It also presents a general method for building non-additive AONTs from linear ones using coordinate-wise symbol permutations. The non-linearity of the resulting instances is measured with differential Δ_F-uniformity and Walsh magnitude, with theoretical conditions and statistical results given.

entry.title: GRID-MRI: Assessing Power System Resilience Against Coordinated Cyber-Physical Attacks
entry.summary: GRID-MRI: Resilience Assessment of Power Systems under Coordinated Cyber-Physical Attacks arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper proposes GRID-MRI, a multidimensional index that measures power system resilience by combining disruption severity, coordination effects, and climatic and economic-regulatory conditions. The framework is applied to a modified IEEE 39-bus system under three escalating cyber-physical attack scenarios inspired by a December 2025 Polish cyberattack. Results show that coordinated attacks cause system collapse, with resilience losses 3.72 and 4.09 times their additive estimates, indicating that simple additive assessments are insufficient.

entry.title: Optimal Tokenization Disambiguation for Secure Linguistic Steganography
entry.summary: Optimal Single-History Tokenization Disambiguation for Provably Secure Linguistic Steganography arXiv · Nov 13, 2026The paper addresses a flaw in provably secure linguistic steganography, where ambiguous tokenizations prevent the receiver from extracting the hidden message reliably. The authors prove that a single-history receiver must give up stop entropy, and they propose coin projection, a closed-form scheme that reaches this bound. Experiments on English, Chinese and Japanese show that coin projection retains 91-93% of string entropy and converts 2.16 to 6.85 times more entropy into message bits than SyncPool. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove a single-history receiver must give up stop entropy, and present a closed-form coin projection scheme attaining this bound, compared against SyncPool on English, Chinese, and Japanes

entry.title: NonSense: A study on whether FPGA anti-tamper sensors can be trusted
entry.summary: NonSense: On the (In)security of FPGA Anti-tamper Sensors arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper examines on-chip sensors that FPGAs use to detect physical attacks such as glitching and trigger responses like key zeroization. The authors argue these sensors are a fragile, underexplored attack surface, and show that their detection and response mechanisms can be bypassed without invasive tampering. They also discuss how power delivery network behavior, temperature, and long-term aging reduce sensor reliability, and propose countermeasures to harden these mechanisms.

entry.title: Infrastructure for verifiable AI: where proof costs come from and how hardware can help
entry.summary: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper examines how users of AI services, including large transformer-based language models, can verify that computation follows its declared procedure without exposing private models or data. The authors propose a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, and measure six provers and seven kernels. They find that the dominant proof cost varies with the proof system and input length. They conclude that effective hardware acceleration depends on matching the choice of hardware and proof-system optimizations to the cost profile of the target workload.

entry.title: Bounds on the share of edited watermarked text
entry.summary: Prevalence Bounds for Edited Watermarked Text: Power Envelopes and Calibration Sensitivity arXiv · Nov 13, 2026The paper addresses how much of a corpus comes from a watermarked language model, a question watermark detectors do not directly answer. For Gumbel-max and KGW green-list watermarks under unknown editing, it derives a power envelope from a least-favourable next-token distribution and sequential coupling, governed by retention, entropy and substitution budgets. It gives identified sets and finite-sample bounds on the share of a fixed corpus. In resampling trials on OPT-1.3B and Qwen3-1.7B text, the bounds mostly covered, but coverage is sensitive to null calibration error.

entry.title: Anonymous in Name Only: Critical Review and Reidentification Test of EU Google Search Data Anonymization
entry.summary: Anonymous in Name Only: A Critical Review and a Reidentification Exercise on the European Commission's Anonymization Measures for Google Search Data under Article 6(11) of the DMA arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper examines anonymization measures the European Commission proposed in July 2026 for Alphabet's Google Search data, which must be shared with competing search engines under Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act. The authors argue the residual risk assessment, suppression thresholds, and reliance on contractual safeguards have significant conceptual flaws. Using real Google Search data, they demonstrate low-effort reidentification, record linkage, and confidential attribute inference. They conclude the measures fail all three anonymization criteria set by the European Data Protection Board and should not be treated as sound practice.

entry.title: Maturity²: Evaluating How Mature Crypto Agility Maturity Models Are
entry.summary: Maturity²: Assessing the Maturity of Crypto Agility Maturity Models arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper evaluates three industry-driven crypto agility maturity models, which help organizations prepare for cryptographic transitions such as migration to post-quantum cryptography. The authors assess the models against established design principles and find recurring weaknesses, notably the lack of measurable, reproducible assessment criteria and limited prescriptive guidance. The paper also highlights individual strengths of the models and offers concrete recommendations for improving future crypto agility maturity models.

entry.title: STEALTH: A hidden-message method that works across different computer hardware
entry.summary: STEALTH: Steganographic Text Encoding Agnostic to Low-Level Tensor Hardware arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper presents STEALTH, a method for hiding secret messages in text generated by a language model, so the text looks like ordinary model output to anyone without the key. The authors show that existing provably secure schemes often fail to decode messages when the receiver's precision, quantization, or GPU differs from the sender's. STEALTH uses keyed pseudorandom noise for token sampling together with a rateless spinal code decoded by beam search to tolerate these differences. The paper reports that every test message was decoded across precisions, smaller models, a different GPU, and different model families, and that trained steganalyzers and a targeted statistical test could not distinguish its stegotexts from honest output.

entry.title: Batch, Pack, and Prove: More Efficient Verifiable Computation for CKKS
entry.summary: Batch, Pack, and Prove: More Efficient Verifiable Computation for CKKS arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper addresses verifying the integrity of encrypted computations in the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme. It introduces a more efficient arithmetization, BatchFold (a polynomial commitment supporting batched evaluations), a packing technique that removes the O(N) range-proof overhead, and SparsePack for proving sparse polynomial evaluations. The authors report proofs several orders of magnitude smaller and faster than prior approaches on a generic neural network architecture.

entry.title: "Look It Up": Multi-bit LLM Watermarking Using Codebook Search
entry.summary: Look It Up: Multi-bit LLM Watermarking via Codebook Search arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper proposes a codebook-based watermarking method for attributing short LLM-generated texts to their source. An n-bit payload is mapped to a longer u-bit codeword, embedded during generation through token-level logit biasing, and recovered by finding the nearest codeword in a secret codebook using Hamming or Levenshtein distance. Experiments report near-perfect recovery of 16 to 24-bit payloads on 200-token generations and strong results on 127-token generations from base models.

entry.title: Faster private decision-tree evaluation on encrypted data using signed dyadic path encoding
entry.summary: Signed Dyadic Path Encoding for Efficient Non-Interactive Private Decision Tree Evaluation over TFHE arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper proposes a signed dyadic path-sum encoding for privately evaluating decision trees over TFHE, where a server classifies an encrypted query without learning its input. The method packs the two children of each leaf-parent into one test polynomial, reducing programmable bootstrapping operations from the number of leaves to the number of leaf-parents. The authors extend the approach to gradient-boosted ensembles and report reduced latency on UCI benchmarks at depths 1 to 4 without accuracy loss.

entry.title: MobileProbe: Adaptive Security Testing of Phone-Operating AI Agents via Trajectory-Aware Injection
entry.summary: MobileProbe: Adaptive Security Evaluation of Mobile Agents via Trajectory-Aware Injection arXiv · Nov 12, 2026Mobile GUI agents operate phone apps for users by reading the screen, so attackers can hide malicious instructions in ordinary interface content to redirect them. This paper proposes MobileProbe, a red-teaming framework that automatically finds attacker-controllable content, locates vulnerable decision points along an agent's execution path, and iteratively refines context-aware attack payloads. The authors built a benchmark of 83 long-horizon attack instances across 12 mobile apps, each labeled with a confidentiality, integrity, or availability goal. Tested on three representative agent architectures, MobileProbe achieved higher attack success rates than human-written, zero-shot LLM, and adapted prior automated baselines.

entry.title: CrossPloit: A Benchmark for Moving Web Exploit Proofs Across Python Versions
entry.summary: CrossPloit: A Benchmark for Cross-Version PoC Migration in Python Web Applications arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper introduces CrossPloit, a benchmark of 127 instances across 45 CVEs in Python web applications, testing whether a proof-of-concept exploit for a listed version can trigger the same vulnerability on an earlier, unlisted version. Benchmark construction identified 149 vulnerable prior versions missing from the affected-version lists of four databases, 127 of which require migration. Across 18 agent configurations, the best resolved 58.3% of instances versus 8.7% for an adapted baseline, while attack-vector shift cases were hardest, with no configuration exceeding 37.9%.

entry.title: Small Decision Models in a Harness Find Memory-Safety Flaws at Scale on Consumer GPUs
entry.summary: Look Here, Then Decide: Small Decision Models in a Harness Find Memory-Safety Vulnerabilities at Scale on Commodity GPUs arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper asks whether small open-weight decision models can support large-scale vulnerability discovery in open-source C and C++ software. A deterministic harness selects projects and localizes suspicious code, and the 4B-parameter Intern-Decision-4B model scores and ranks candidate functions rather than making final accept or reject decisions. On 75 public CVEs, the fixed function reached its repository's top 25 in 21% of cases, about 1.4 times the rate of random ordering. The campaign confirmed 187 memory-safety findings, with 12 rated critical under worst-case CVSS v3.1.

entry.title: Game-theory study of RIS-assisted challenge-response physical-layer authentication, Part I: perfect channel knowledge
entry.summary: Game-Theoretic Analysis of RIS-Assisted Challenge-Response PLA - Part I: Perfect Channel Knowledge arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies a physical-layer authentication setting where a user Alice communicates with an authenticator Bob through a reconfigurable intelligent surface controlled by Bob, while an attacker Trudy tries to impersonate Alice by precoding her messages. Under perfect channel knowledge, the authors model the joint RIS selection and precoder design as a finite zero-sum game, deriving exact channel subspace conditions for attack indistinguishability and equilibrium mixed strategies. Simulations in geometric and 3GPP UMi-NLOS channels show that authentication performance depends on spatial degrees of freedom, channel correlation, and SNR, and that the proposed strategies balance rate and security better than conventional benchmarks.

entry.title: Verifiable approximate nearest neighbor search in outsourced vector databases
entry.summary: Authenticated Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in Outsourced Vector Databases arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper addresses how to verify the integrity of approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search results when vector databases are outsourced to third-party clouds, where untrusted providers might return suboptimal or fabricated results. The authors propose VIDA, which replaces raw vector transmission with compact vector commitments and uses an aggregated Inner Product Argument to verify multiple distance computations efficiently. They also introduce MeST, a topology-aware authenticated data structure, and a quantization-aware strategy that uses distance bounds for pruning. Experiments report up to a 6.6× end-to-end latency speedup and up to 99.2% reduction in data transfer time compared with state-of-the-art methods.

entry.title: How to Defeat a Mafia of Size 1: A Provably Optimal Strategy for the Detective in a Social Deduction Game
entry.summary: How to Defeat a Mafia (of Size 1) arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies the social deduction game Mafia, in which players try to identify a secret coalition among them, with one non-coalition player acting as a Detective with special abilities. The authors analyse the case with one mafia member and one detective. They describe an explicit strategy that is provably optimal, providing a first such example beyond the case without a Detective.

entry.title: Bait: A defense against harmful agentic reinforcement learning by probing the reward function
entry.summary: Bait: Mitigating Harmful Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Probing Reward Function arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper shows that safety alignment of a large language model can be fully undone through harmful agentic reinforcement learning run via a service API, at a cost of about $20. The authors propose Bait, a defense that proactively probes the reward function to block learning from harmful rewards. Experiments indicate Bait still allows learning from benign reward functions, and analysis suggests an adaptive attacker aware of Bait cannot perfectly subvert it. ★★★★ Notable: The authors expose a safety vulnerability in agentic RL services and propose Bait, a defense probing the reward function; experiments report mitigation of harmful learning.

entry.title: ReliaGuard: Reconstruction-Aware Watermarking for Tracing Image Sources and Locating Edits
entry.summary: ReliaGuard: Reconstruction-Aware Watermarking for Source Attribution and Blind Edit Localization arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper presents ReliaGuard, a watermarking framework for identifying the source of generated or edited images and locating edited regions without a reference. The writer embeds keyed features into both the protected image and its variational autoencoder reconstruction, while the reader uses only the received image and a secret key to predict an edit mask. On an independent test set of 300 source images and 900 editing cases from three image domains, edit-region IoU reaches 85.61% for complete outputs and 94.90% for locally spliced outputs, with identifier-bit accuracy at 100% in both conditions.

entry.title: SEC: A Secret Sharing Scheme Giving Each Participant One Short Share
entry.summary: SEC: One-Share Everywhere-Short Secret Sharing from Lossless Expanders arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper introduces SEC, a ramp secret sharing scheme built from lossless bipartite expander graphs, aimed at lattice-based distributed cryptography. Each participant receives exactly one share regardless of the number of parties or thresholds, and shares and reconstruction vectors have bounded coefficients. The authors define hard-core local leakage resilience and prove SEC satisfies it under the MatrixHint-MLWE problem.

entry.title: Optimal feature selection for firewall log analysis using machine learning and hybrid metaheuristics
entry.summary: Optimal feature selection for firewall log analysis using Machine learning and Hybrid Metaheuristic algorithms arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper proposes bee swarm optimization with Q-learning-based local search (QBSO-FS) to select features for classifying firewall logs in the UCI Internet Firewall Data Set. The method is paired with random forest, k-nearest neighbor, and Bernoulli naive Bayes classifiers. Using a leakage-free split into training, validation, and test sets, random forest with 7 selected features on deduplicated data reaches 99.90% accuracy and 94.88% Macro-F1. Evaluation over multiple splits is left as future work.

entry.title: PolicySniff: a side-channel attack that infers an LLM agent's approval-policy setting from shared-GPU timing
entry.summary: PolicySniff: Inferring Agent Policy States through Shared-GPU Execution arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper presents PolicySniff, a method by which a co-resident attacker on the same GPU infers which approval-policy setting an LLM agent is using, by timing only its own GPU kernels. On an eager sparse mixture-of-experts runtime, it identified the deployed setting with 94.17% balanced accuracy. The authors conclude that behavioral compliance does not imply configuration confidentiality, so operators should measure distinguishability on their serving runtime and enforce authorization outside the model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show GPU-sharing timing side channels can infer an LLM agent's approval policy, reporting 94.17% balanced accuracy on a sparse MoE runtime.

entry.title: Fault injection attacks on Q-learning: how hardware glitches can break reinforcement learning and how to defend it
entry.summary: Fault Injection Attacks on Q-Learning: Analysis, Vulnerabilities, and Countermeasures arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper analyzes how hardware fault injection attacks, using voltage and clock glitching on a ChipWhisperer platform, affect five Q-Learning variants. Standard implementations are corrupted during both learning and inference, and the Robust variant still retains injected NaN and infinite values. The Resilient variant, using triple modular redundancy with majority voting, corrects corruption in a single Q-table copy but leaves shared inputs such as the reward and the voting code unprotected. In a traffic light control simulation, a single injected infinite value degraded accumulated vehicle waiting time by 148x, while triple modular redundancy corrected the faults injected in the tests.

entry.title: CoordX Types: A Trustless, Swappable Type System for Shared Records
entry.summary: CoordX Types: A Trustless, Swappable Type System for Shared Records arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The CoordX Protocol verifies who wrote each signed, encrypted entry and whether they had permission, but it does not define what entries mean. This paper presents the CoordX type system, which assigns meaning through short documents that specify how to read parts of a shared record. Types are signed objects fixed by their digest, and each party evaluates them independently over verified entries, so no trust in a server or other party is required. A type names its intended interpreter, allowing several interpreters to coexist within one record.

entry.title: Intent-aware protection for AI agents: using deployed purpose as a security reference
entry.summary: Intent-Aware Protection for AI Agents arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper notes that existing defenses mainly detect prompt injection or harmful outputs and cannot tell whether an AI agent still serves its deployed purpose. The authors propose Intent-Aware Security, defining Intent Preservation and Intent Drift through an Intent Profile built from organizational, role, and developer intent. They present an 887-sample benchmark across 35 agents and four profile-based protections, which outperform profile-free baselines on their evaluations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors treat trusted agent intent as a security object, define intent drift, and report gains over baselines on their benchmark and AgentDojo trajectories.

entry.title: Hiding Targets in 6G Sensing Using Environmental Scatterers
entry.summary: Harnessing Environmental Scatterers for Endogenous Target Covertness in 6G ISAC: A New Paradigm for Sensing Security arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper examines security threats in 6G integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems, noting that existing methods mainly reduce a warden's parameter-estimation accuracy rather than hiding a target's presence. The authors propose endogenous target covertness, which uses known objects, ambient backscatter devices, and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces as ghost targets to make the true target hard for a warden to detect. The legitimate base station can still extract the true target's response using prior knowledge of the scatterers. A case study shows that target covertness can be achieved without dedicated jamming power, and open research challenges are outlined.

entry.title: Hiding Targets from Wireless Sensing Detection Using Reconfigurable-Antenna Reflectors
entry.summary: Low Probability of Target Detection in Wireless Sensing by Harnessing Reconfigurable-antenna based Reflectors arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper introduces low probability of target detection (LPTD) as a security goal for wireless sensing, aiming to conceal a target's existence from passive wardens. The authors deploy reconfigurable-antenna reflectors around the target as artificial scatterers, adjusting their reflection coefficients to mask the target's echo. They analyze the warden's optimal detection strategy, derive false-alarm and missed-detection probabilities, and give a closed-form minimum total detection error probability. Numerical results show that sufficient reflector cooperation raises this error probability to about 0.94 to 0.96, close to random guessing.

entry.title: Optimal integer masks limiting one-guess attacks under a mask-cost budget
entry.summary: Optimal Additive Integer Masks for One-Guess Vulnerability under an Absolute-Moment Budget arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper studies the average one-guess success probability of an adversary who observes the integer sum of a finite-support secret and an independent integer mask, with the mask's absolute moment bounded. For a uniform secret on an interval, the exact optimum and an explicit optimiser are obtained. For a biased bit, the paper characterises masks that do not increase success over the prior baseline, determines their minimal cost, and gives the full cost-vulnerability frontier for every bias. ★★★★ Notable: The authors exactly characterise the cost-vulnerability frontier of additive integer masks, showing infinitely many piecewise-linear pieces accumulating at a critical cost, for uniform and biased-bit

entry.title: Study of privacy leakage from recurrent state in LLM inference
entry.summary: Privacy Leakage from Recurrent State in LLM Inference arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies how personalized LLM services compress private context into fixed-size recurrent state that can still be inferred after public dialogue. The authors probe partial states and observe GPU power during inference across released hybrid models. They find that private facts and personal attributes can be recovered and can change later decisions, and that whole-device power can reveal information such as age. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend recurrent-state privacy leakage to persistence and GPU power side channels, reporting probing experiments and an unprivileged age inference on a partitioned GPU, affecting serving a

entry.title: Auditing feature attribution for network intrusion detection by restricting queries to protocol-valid network states
entry.summary: Protocol-Aware Auditing of Domain-Blind Feature Attribution in Network Intrusion Detection arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper argues that feature-attribution methods can query network states that violate protocol rules, so explanations and their evaluation depend on model behavior outside the operational domain. The authors formalize this as domain blindness and prove that a procedure confined to a declared rule-valid set returns the same attribution when models agree on the required information within that set. They apply a protocol-aware query-control principle to LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, and DeepLIFT and audit these configurations across four network intrusion detection datasets and three classifier families.

entry.title: DUFT: Device-unique feedback traversal for generating authentication responses from SRAM PUFs
entry.summary: DUFT: Device-Unique Feedback Traversal for Entropy-Estimated Response Extraction and Mutual Authentication using SRAM PUFs arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper proposes DUFT (Device-Unique Feedback Traversal), a seed-based, multi-round feedback mechanism built on SRAM physical unclonable functions to produce measured responses. The feedback chain is driven by the device's stable and unstable bit positions and a device key hashed from the SRAM array. The authors report reaching an estimated 128 bits of min-entropy on their reference hardware, and use the mechanism in a lightweight authentication and key-encapsulation protocol evaluated on physical IoT and embedded hardware.

entry.title: Privacy-protecting obfuscation of spectrum data for next-generation spectrum sharing systems
entry.summary: Privacy-Preserving Spectrum Data Obfuscation in Next-Generation Spectrum Coexistence Systems arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies how to protect privacy when partially disclosing primary user spectrum usage in spectrum coexistence systems. It shows that naive randomized subset disclosures can leak spectrum information through inference that exploits temporal structure. The authors design structure-aware obfuscation schemes for Markovian and periodic usage dynamics that disrupt inference, and report that these schemes significantly hinder recovery of spectrum information.

entry.title: Beyond the Diff: VulSpot, a vulnerability dataset that locates every vulnerability
entry.summary: Beyond the Diff - VulSpot: A Vulnerability Dataset Where No Vulnerability Goes Unlocalized arXiv · Nov 12, 2026VulSpot is a continuously refreshed benchmark for detecting, classifying, and localizing software vulnerabilities. It contains over 500k functions in 21 languages, drawn from 24k registered CVEs, including over 15k vulnerable C/C++ functions. By linking code added by a patch to the existing statement it protects, it locates the vulnerability in 99.3% of functions that earlier diff-based datasets could not localize. It also reports how reliable each label is, offers leak-free splits and hierarchical CWE labels, and is updated automatically every month.

entry.title: Hidden Image Attacks: Recovering Secret Content from Deep Hiding Models
entry.summary: Your Secrets Are Showing: Deep Image Hiding Models Are Surprisingly Easy to Attack arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper examines whether an attacker can identify what a hidden image depicts without knowing which model concealed it. The authors built a dataset from 11 deep hiding models and trained a single decoder that extracts secret content from unseen models, recognizable by both humans and machines. The attack also works on out-of-distribution secrets, multi-image hiding, and exposes private content hidden by AIRPNet. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show a single decoder extracts hidden secrets across 11 deep hiding models, strengthened via frequency-guided training, with implications for steganographic privacy.

entry.title: A legal taxonomy of synthetic data sorting it into three types by how it is generated
entry.summary: Taxonomizing Synthetic Data for Law arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper examines the legal and policy issues raised by synthetic data, arguing it should not be treated as wholly separate from collected real data. Building on Gal and Lynskey's taxonomy, the authors divide synthetic data into transformed, augmented, and simulated categories based on background knowledge and ground-truth assumptions. They find that no category prevents group-based inference privacy harms, that augmented and simulated data can amplify bias, and that synthetic data rarely helps smaller competitors overcome incumbents' data advantages.

entry.title: What You See Is (Not) What You Got: How People Are Fooled by PDF Signatures
entry.summary: What You See Is (Not) What You Got: The Human Factor in PDF Signature Verification arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper introduces Genuine PDF Forgeries, an attack that exploits the gap between cryptographically verified signer certificates and the signature blocks people see in PDF documents. The authors tested 23 PDF viewers and validation tools, finding that nine of the 13 that automatically report validity hide authenticated signer details behind extra user actions. Online studies with 584 EU participants and a real-world test within two organizations assessed how often the forged visual identity was accepted. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a new attack class exploiting mismatches between visible signature blocks and certificates, tested on 23 viewers and 584 participants.

entry.title: HARE: Faster Read Disturbance Threshold Profiling in DRAM Chips
entry.summary: HARE: Fast Read Disturbance Threshold Profiling in Modern DRAM Chips via Reduced Timing Constraints arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper presents HARE, an online profiling technique for measuring the read disturbance threshold (RDT) of modern DRAM chips, which is the minimum number of row activations that causes the first bitflip. HARE reduces the timing constraints between consecutive DRAM commands during profiling, which shortens profiling time and intensifies read disturbance. Characterization of 180 DDR4 chips reports that HARE measures a row's RDT 31.2% faster than the RowHammer profiler and flips more than 95% of the cells that the RowHammer pattern flips.

entry.title: Chinese Whispers About Vulnerabilities: How Online Accounts of the Same Flaws Diverge
entry.summary: Chinese Whispers About Vulnerabilities arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper analyzes about 382 thousand online references to roughly 55 thousand software vulnerabilities to compare how similar the information sources are. It finds that the sources are mostly statistically dissimilar, with a mean cosine similarity of only 0.22. Vulnerabilities tied to GitHub and programming language ecosystems, and vulnerability reports, tend to show even more dissimilarity.

entry.title: Weak unit reducibility of the eleventh cyclotomic field
entry.summary: Weak Unit Reducibility of the Eleventh Cyclotomic Field arXiv · Nov 11, 2026The paper proves that the cyclotomic field K11 = Q(ζ11) is unit reducible but not strongly unit reducible. As a result, every nonzero principal fractional ideal of this field has a generator that is a shortest nonzero vector. The paper also gives results on norms of shortest vectors in the ideal hO_K11.

entry.title: Full-mesh dynamic four-user entanglement-based QKD network integrated with an SD-KMS
entry.summary: Full Mesh Dynamic Four-User Entanglement-based Switched QKD Network Integrated with SD-KMS arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper demonstrates a reconfigurable quantum key distribution network with four users in a full-mesh topology, using polarization entanglement. The network is integrated with a software-defined key management system that coordinates dynamic optical switching and real-time key provisioning for quantum-safe applications.

entry.title: SecDVA: A Secure Multi-Party Framework for Valuing Data in Machine Learning Markets
entry.summary: SecDVA: A Maliciously Secure Multi-Party Framework for Data Value Assessment in Modern Machine Learning Data Markets arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper presents SecDVA, a multi-party computation framework that lets buyers assess how much a seller's data would improve a machine learning model before purchase. It keeps the seller's data and the buyer's model and test data private beyond the final valuation result, and remains robust against malicious participants. To make this practical for large models, it uses neural tangent kernel linearization and mini-batch approximations to reduce computation. Experiments reported in the paper show it outperforms existing baselines in plaintext settings and handles large-scale models in reasonable time under MPC.

entry.title: IoTPwnBench: A Benchmark for Testing IoT Firmware Security Tools
entry.summary: IoTPwnBench: A Synthetic Benchmark for IoT Firmware Security Analysis arXiv · Nov 11, 2026IoTPwnBench is a synthetic, modular benchmark for evaluating security analysis tools on IoT firmware. It contains 716 vulnerable firmware images covering 86 weakness scenarios and 28 CWE classes across 11 device profiles. Each vulnerable image has a corrected twin, allowing researchers to compare detection results and false positives before and after the weakness is removed.

entry.title: Browser Immune System: In-Browser Threat Detection with a Security Transformer
entry.summary: Browser Immune System (BIS): Innate and Adaptive Threat Detection in the Browser with a Cybersecurity Transformer arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper presents the Browser Immune System (BIS), a browser extension that screens web navigation for threats using alias-web, a 4-billion-parameter cybersecurity transformer running on the user's GPU. The model is quantised to 4 bits and compiled for WebGPU, answering a typed security question in about 150 ms. On BISBENCH-8, a benchmark of eight synthetic sites, BIS returned the expected verdict on 7 of 8 sites with a class-level micro-F1 of 0.71, and the authors report all errors, including false positives on some real public pages.

entry.title: Affine combiners for Reed-Solomon proximity gaps
entry.summary: Affine Combiners for Reed-Solomon Proximity Gaps arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper studies proximity gaps for Reed-Solomon codes, which underpin the soundness of protocols that test received words via random combinations. The authors propose affine combiners that merge two received words as f(x)+(α+βx)g(x) and prove mutual correlated agreement with error O(1/q+n²/q²). For q≥n², this error is O(1/q), an asymptotic factor-n improvement over the Ω(n/q) error of scalar combiners. The result is extended to k-variate Reed-Muller codes on subfield grids. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose affine combiners achieving MCA error O(1/q), claiming a factor-n improvement over scalar combiners for Reed-Solomon proximity gaps.

entry.title: Reprogramming dormant neurons to backdoor AI agents
entry.summary: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents arXiv · Nov 11, 2026The paper introduces Lazarus, a method that edits fewer than ten dormant neurons in a model's final feed-forward block, without training, so that a trigger string in the agent's context makes it emit a chosen payload. On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, seven edited neurons fired the payload on at least 98.8% of triggered test trajectories, with no observed leakage on the evaluated benign trajectories, and similar vulnerability was reported for Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT. The authors report that agent-built defenses flagged 91.4% of edited checkpoints at a 9.7% false positive rate, and argue that model weights should be audited before deployment and monitored afterward. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a training-free backdoor editing fewer than ten dormant neurons, tested on three models with 23 trigger trajectories.

entry.title: One Fabrication Is Enough: How a Fake News Article Changes LLM Forecasts
entry.summary: One Fabrication Is Enough: A Fake News Article Changes the Forecasts of LLM Forecasting Systems arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper studies how large language model forecasting systems that retrieve news as evidence can be manipulated. An attacker who knows only the forecasting question and publishes a fabricated article, without access to the model or retriever, can reverse 74% to 82% of opposing forecasts across frontier models tested. Retrieval of the fake article occurs in about 90% of runs for two leading deployed systems. The authors also evaluate two published retrieval-time defenses and report that each is bypassed or discards substantial genuine news. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors show a weakest attacker publishing fake news can reverse forecasts and bypass retrieval defenses, reporting tests on stock and prediction-market questions across frontier models.

entry.title: obfsgen: A generative-model approach to hiding tunnel traffic shape
entry.summary: obfsgen: Generative Tunnel Obfuscation arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper presents obfsgen, a schedule-driven obfuscator for encrypted tunnel traffic that aims to evade censors who detect circumvention by traffic shape. It samples when and how much to send from a generative sequence model of normal traffic that predicts a flow's future shape from its full history. The paper also addresses practical system issues such as synchronization over noisy networks and evaluates distinguishability, performance overhead, and computational requirements. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a schedule-driven tunnel obfuscator sampling send timing from a generative sequence model against TLS traffic-shape fingerprints, reporting evaluation of indistinguishability, over

entry.title: Protecting Sensitive Knowledge in LLM Unlearning Against Proxy Attacks
entry.summary: Protecting Sensitive Knowledge Under LLM Unlearning: The Proxy Threat and a Superposition-Aware Defense arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper shows that representations of different entities in a large language model can overlap in shared parameters, so removing one entity may affect others. The authors define the Proxy Unlearning Attack, in which legitimate removal requests are used to erase sensitive entities that were never requested. They propose Superposition-Aware Unlearning Protection, a defense that detects at-risk entities before unlearning and decouples and restores affected entities afterward.

entry.title: VRMaaS: Verifiable Reward-Model-as-a-Service for Trustworthy LLM Alignment
entry.summary: VRMaaS: Verifiable Reward-Model-as-a-Service for Trustworthy LLM Alignment arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper addresses reward models used as remote services in LLM alignment pipelines, where their scores drive payment and governance decisions. It proposes VRMaaS, a framework that attaches a proof to each returned reward, letting auditors confirm the score matches the intended request, model checkpoint, numerical configuration, and verifier without rerunning the private model. A GPU prototype on 1B, 3B, and 8B reward models reports 93.5-99% pairwise agreement with the baseline and rejects every tested service-field substitution.

entry.title: Hijacking a Trusted LLM in Quantized Deployment via a Disguised LoRA Adapter
entry.summary: Hijacking a Trusted LLM in Real-World Quantized Deployments Only Requires a Disguised Adapter arXiv · Nov 11, 2026The paper presents QHijack-LoRA, an attack in which a third-party LoRA adapter behaves benignly with the full-precision base model but hijacks decisions once that base is quantized for deployment. The attacker modifies neither the trusted base model nor the victim's quantization configuration. The authors also propose a cross-precision paired audit that checks adapters in their intended quantized deployment configuration.

entry.title: Poison-then-Hide: a backdoor attack that hides in pretrained vision encoders and activates during finetuning
entry.summary: Poison-then-Hide: Finetuning-Activated Backdoor Attack on Pretrained Vision Encoders arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper proposes Poison-then-Hide, an attack that implants a dormant backdoor in a pretrained vision encoder, which is activated when the model is later finetuned on clean downstream data. The method combines trigger optimization, base encoder poisoning, and targeted unlearning to conceal the backdoor. Tested on six datasets and three architectures, it reaches attack success rates up to 97%. The authors report that standard detection and mitigation defenses cannot fully remove the backdoor, which can reappear after benign finetuning.

entry.title: Speech tokenizers are vulnerable to transferable semantic attacks; a robust tokenizer is proposed
entry.summary: Speech Tokenizers are Vulnerable: Transferable Semantic Attack and Robust Tokenizer arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper shows that speech tokenizers, which encode speech for downstream ASR and audio-language models, are fragile at the semantic level. The authors propose T-SemAttack, which jointly shifts the representations of several semantic encoders to disrupt speech content while preserving perceptual quality, degrading downstream performance. They also introduce ROSETok, a robust speech tokenizer built with noisy training and robust semantic distillation, and report experiments across multiple datasets, ASR systems and audio-language models. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a transferable semantic attack on speech tokenizers and a robust tokenizer, evaluated on nine ASR systems and four LALMs.

entry.title: Delegatable keyed-verification anonymous credentials
entry.summary: Delegatable Keyed-Verification Anonymous Credentials IACR ePrint · Nov 11, 2026This paper proposes the first delegatable keyed-verification anonymous credentials (DKVAC). Keyed-verification anonymous credentials are used when the issuer and verifier are the same or mutually trusted, avoiding the need for bilinear pairings. The authors give formal definitions, design two pairing-free constructions that support delegation, prove their security, and benchmark their implementations. The two constructions trade off expressiveness against performance.

entry.title: Shortest-vector problem in infinity norm is NP-hard for power-of-two cyclotomic ideals
entry.summary: mathsfSVP_∞ Is NP-Hard for Power-of-two Cyclotomic Ideals IACR ePrint · Nov 11, 2026This paper proves that exact decision shortest vector problem (SVP) in the coefficient infinity norm is NP-complete for principal ideals and rank-two free modules over cyclotomic rings Z[X]/(X^n+1) with n a power of two. For each case, it gives a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from Subset Sum. The results are transferred to the cyclic rings Z[X]/(X^{2n}-1), establishing NP-completeness for free modules of any fixed positive rank over these rings. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give deterministic polynomial-time reductions from Subset Sum, proving NP-hardness of l-infinity SVP for power-of-two cyclotomic ideals and modules.

entry.title: A note improving the KLPT2 algorithm's output size and degree bound
entry.summary: An improvement to the KLPT2 algorithm IACR ePrint · Nov 11, 2026This short note tweaks the KLPT2 algorithm to reduce its output size from O(p^15.5) to Õ(p^14.5). It then shows that a recent improvement to the KLPT algorithm by Nakagawa, Yoshizumi and Onuki is compatible with the Hermitian module splitting approach. Combining the two lowers the reduced degree bound to Õ(p^14).

entry.title: Affine combiners for Reed-Solomon proximity gaps (a cryptography paper on a new way to combine received words so that random tests of codes have smaller error)
entry.summary: Affine Combiners for Reed-Solomon Proximity Gaps IACR ePrint · Nov 11, 2026This paper studies proximity gaps for Reed-Solomon codes, where protocols test received words through random combinations. It proposes affine combiners that merge two words f and g as f(x)+(α+βx)g(x) with random α, β. The authors prove mutual correlated agreement with one coordinate of agreement loss, with error O(1/q+n²/q²), and show an asymptotic factor-n improvement over scalar combiners. The results are also extended to multivariate Reed-Muller codes on subfield grids. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose affine combiners achieving MCA error O(1/q+n²/q²), a factor-n improvement over scalar combiners for q≥n² near the Johnson threshold.

entry.title: Tightly secure, modular post-quantum TLS handshakes
entry.summary: Tightly Secure and Modular Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes IACR ePrint · Nov 11, 2026This paper presents a unified, tight, and modular reduction framework for post-quantum TLS 1.3 in the standard model and for KEMTLS in the random oracle model. The framework reduces protocol security tightly to the security of an ephemeral KEM, HKDF, and a signature scheme or static KEM. Instantiated with LWE-based schemes, it yields the first (almost) tightly secure constructions of both protocols under the LWE assumption. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors give a unified tight reduction framework for PQ TLS 1.3 and KEMTLS, plus first QROM MU-(dual)-PRF bounds for HMAC and HKDF, yielding near-tight LWE-based instantiations.

entry.title: HIT: One-Pass Inference for Single-Trace NTT Side-Channel Attacks
entry.summary: HIT: Single-Pass Inference for Single-Trace NTT Side-Channel Attacks IACR ePrint · Nov 11, 2026This paper addresses single-trace side-channel key recovery attacks on the Number-Theoretic Transform (NTT) used in the post-quantum standards ML-KEM and ML-DSA. It proposes the Hierarchical Inference Tree (HIT), which merges and prunes candidate inputs from leaves to root in one pass on an acyclic binary tree instead of using loopy belief propagation. The authors report that on ML-KEM-768 it runs over 900 times faster than prior SASCA methods with more than double the noise tolerance, and it enables the first single-trace analytical attack on the ML-DSA NTT. ★★★★ Notable: Replaces loopy belief propagation with a single pass on an acyclic tree, enabling the first single-trace analytical attack on ML-DSA NTT; the authors report experiments on ML-KEM-768 and ARM Cortex-M4

entry.title: Anamorphic NIZK: Definition, Construction and More
entry.summary: Anamorphic NIZK: Definition, Construction and More IACR ePrint · Nov 11, 2026This paper introduces anamorphic non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs (ANIZK), in which publicly verifiable proofs can carry covert messages recoverable only with a double key. It formalizes anamorphic security, strong robustness, and recipient anamorphic zero knowledge with simulation extractability. A generic construction in the random oracle model is given, and applying it within the Naor-Yung paradigm yields recipient anamorphic encryption. An asymmetric variant, ASY-ANIZK, is also proposed.

entry.title: Collision attacks on SHA-2 reaching 39 steps below the birthday bound
entry.summary: Collision Attacks on SHA-2: 39-Step SHA-256 below the Birthday Bound IACR ePrint · Nov 11, 2026This paper studies collision attacks on the SHA-2 hash family and introduces joint message-word pinning, which fixes two expanded message words. The authors estimate that collisions for 39-step SHA-256 can be found below the 2^128 birthday bound by keeping an existing characteristic and changing how its conditions are satisfied. For 38-step SHA-256, a new differential characteristic lowers the estimated cost from 2^104.3 to 2^90.9. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce joint message-word pinning, reducing 39-step SHA-256 collision cost to 2^108.8, below the birthday bound.

entry.title: Bulletproofs Are Optimal: Lower Bounds for Vector Commitments in Pairing-Free Groups
entry.summary: Bulletproofs are Optimal: Lower Bounds for Vector Commitments from Fiat-Shamir in Pairing-Free Groups IACR ePrint · Nov 11, 2026This paper examines how efficient vector commitments can be in pairing-free prime-order groups. Existing state-of-the-art schemes combine generalized Pedersen commitments with inner product arguments, yielding proofs of Θ(log n) group elements. The authors work in Maurer's Generic Group Model and prove that any accumulator with interactive public-coin membership proofs must incur a cost in commitment size, opening proof size, or proof length. The bound also extends to related primitives such as polynomial and functional commitments. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove lower bounds in Maurer's generic group model for accumulators and vector commitments in pairing-free prime-order groups, implying that Bulletproofs-style constructions are essentiall

entry.title: Sharper Noise Bounds for Polynomial Evaluation in BGV Homomorphic Encryption
entry.summary: From Dependent Ciphertexts to Sharp Bounds for Polynomial Evaluation in BGV IACR ePrint · Nov 12, 2026This paper presents the first average-case noise analysis for the BGV fully homomorphic encryption scheme that accounts for correlations from secret and public keys as well as dependencies between ciphertexts. The authors propose new variance estimates for noise in homomorphic additions and multiplications and extend the framework to polynomial evaluation. Their estimates match experiments within 1.2 bits, and they use them to select smaller initial ciphertext moduli than those in OpenFHE and HElib. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present the first average-case noise analysis for BGV accounting for key and ciphertext dependencies, extending it to polynomial evaluation and smaller moduli.

entry.title: BMRaccoon: Lattice-Based Blind Multi-Signatures for Post-Quantum Security
entry.summary: BMRaccoon: Blind Multi-Signatures from Lattices IACR ePrint · Nov 12, 2026This paper presents BMRaccoon, the first lattice-based post-quantum blind multi-signature scheme, allowing a user to obtain a compact signature on a hidden message from multiple signers. Its two-round signing protocol is secure under concurrent sessions, and its signatures are compatible with Raccoon. The authors also introduce MRaccoon, a Raccoon-based multi-signature scheme, and prove its strong unforgeability in the random oracle and KOSK models. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present the first lattice-based post-quantum blind multi-signature and first Raccoon-based multi-signature, with security proofs under AOM-MISIS and MSIS and concrete parameters.

entry.title: Extra Privacy Cost of Geometry in Distance-Sensitive Filters: ℓ∞ versus ℓ2
entry.summary: The Price of Geometry for Private Distance-Sensitive Filters: ℓ_∞ versus ℓ₂ IACR ePrint · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies how much extra differential-privacy cost a set representation incurs beyond exact membership when it must accept nearby points and reject distant ones in a metric space. It gives lower bounds that apply to every mechanism, showing an extra cost of Θ_c(d) in ℓ∞ for c<3, which confirms a recent conjecture. In ℓ2 the extra cost is Θ_c(min(d, ln(1/α))), so partition-based constructions are optimal in ℓ∞ but not in ℓ2. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give lower bounds for all private distance-sensitive set representations, separating ℓ∞ (Θ(d)) from ℓ2 (Θ(min(d, ln(1/α)))) and introducing a single-large-ball mechanism.

entry.title: Single-trace power attack on AIMer v3, a Korean post-quantum signature
entry.summary: A Single-Trace Side-Channel Attack on the KpqC Digital Signature Scheme AIMer v3 IACR ePrint · Nov 10, 2026This paper presents a side-channel attack on AIMer v3, a post-quantum digital signature scheme selected in the Korean KpqC competition. The authors use deep learning on a single power trace to exploit leakage of secret preimage bits during computation of the input affine layer. On an ARM Cortex-M4 processor, the full secret key is recovered from one signature with a 100% success rate. The paper also evaluates attack performance under different noise levels and proposes countermeasures.

entry.title: Incrementally verifiable computation that relies on external oracles
entry.summary: Incrementally Verifiable Oracle Aided Computation arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper studies incrementally verifiable computation (IVC), where a prover keeps a short proof that is updated after each step without re-running earlier steps. Under the LWE assumption, the authors build SNARGs and extend them to IVC for computations that query external oracles. For bounded-space computations with robustness, they give privately verifiable constructions and a lower bound against public verifiability. For oracles that sign their answers, they give publicly verifiable constructions without a robustness assumption. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct LWE-based incrementally verifiable oracle-aided computation schemes and a matching lower bound for two settings, reporting public parameter and proof length bounds.

entry.title: When AI Agent Evaluators Disagree: A Study Comparing Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Boundary Checks
entry.summary: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper compares three ways of evaluating AI agents that use tools to read and write data: native scoring against a gold database state, LLM judges, and a minimal rule-based boundary check. The authors ran 2,160 episodes on tau2-bench airline and retail domains and had two annotators label 120 episodes. The LLM judge agreed with native scoring only 56.2% of the time, while the rule-based check caught all 11 forbidden writes that the judges largely missed. The authors conclude that the choice of evaluator determines the conclusion reached. ★★★★ Notable: The authors compare native scoring, LLM judges, and a rule-based boundary check on tau2-bench, reporting that judges miss forbidden writes the minimal check catches. Experiments span 2,160 episodes, w

entry.title: SideTaskBench: Testing Whether Coding Agents Deliver Unrequested Extra Work
entry.summary: SideTaskBench: Measuring Unauthorized Side-Task Delivery in Coding Agents arXiv · Oct 29, 2026This paper introduces SideTaskBench, a benchmark that measures whether coding agents produce unrequested side-task artifacts while repairing a user's code, when third-party technical references prompt them to do so. It pairs 25 Python repairs with 190 side-task units, defining 300 executable repair–side-task pairs across four similarity levels. Experiments show that under wrapped requests, two models delivered roughly 40% valid side tasks while their repair success stayed close to clean baselines. ★★★★ Notable: The authors pair repair tasks with self-contained side tasks and measure both delivery and repair rates. The abstract reports results across 25 repairs, 300 pairs, and 2,400 runs.

entry.title: Detecting Social Engineering Attacks in Corporate Communications via Manipulation Cues
entry.summary: Social Engineering Attack Detection in Corporate Communications arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper studies social engineering attacks in corporate email, chat, and phone communications, which are hard to tell apart from authentic messages. Using real-world datasets, the authors build baseline machine-learning models, and their TF-IDF models classify phishing and safe emails with accuracy above 90%. They also derive lexicon-based indicators of urgency, trust, greed, and other persuasion cues, evaluate them alone to reach a ROC-AUC of 0.74 on a held-out test split, and test whether these features transfer to held-out email sources.

entry.title: FOE-Dreamer: Efficiently Learning Cyber Defense Policies in Live Networks
entry.summary: FOE-Dreamer: Deployment-Efficient Learning of Cyber Defense Policies in Operational Networks arXiv · Nov 11, 2026FOE-Dreamer is a model-based reinforcement learning framework that trains a cyber defender online, directly in a cloud network, without a simulator stage. It separates the latent state into a component controlled by defender actions, an exogenous component driven by benign user activity, and an opponent embedding inferred from defender-observable signals. Tested on an 8-host OpenStack testbed with user activity emulated by GHOSTS against two scripted attacker profiles, it trains within a 3-day budget on a single GPU. Under matched compute, it achieves about 2x better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN baselines.

entry.title: When AI Agents' Caution Becomes a Weakness: Attacks That Trigger Unnecessary Refusals
entry.summary: When Safety Becomes an Attack Surface: Manipulating Abstention in Tool-Using AI Agents arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper studies an availability attack in which adversaries plant fabricated risk warnings in low-trust content to make tool-using AI agents abstain from legitimate tasks. The authors propose a Verify-Before-Abstain protocol that checks warnings against authoritative records or the underlying content. Across three model families and 51 task pairs, caution-first prompting amplified the attack, raising induced over-abstention for Gemini from 9.8% to 86.3%. Provenance-aware verification improved legitimate completion but depended on authoritative evidence.

entry.title: What an RF fingerprint identifies: hardware family or individual device
entry.summary: What Does an RF Fingerprint Identify? A Cross-Corpus Evaluation of Hardware-Family-Associated and Unit-Level Signal arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper examines whether radio-frequency fingerprinting classifiers separate individual transmitters or only their hardware families. The authors compare real hardware groupings against size-matched random groupings using cross-fitted variational lower bounds on unseen devices. Hardware-family groupings exceeded all 999 random groupings on the WiSig Wi-Fi and LoRa corpora. A temperature-calibrated held-out bound of +3.338 bits on 122 ESP32 radios indicates substantial device-specific identity signal.

entry.title: OverServe: Tool–prompt co-designed attacks that inflate resource use of SaaS agents
entry.summary: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper presents OverServe, a multi-agent framework that builds attacks against software-as-a-service agents. It pairs Model Context Protocol status tools with completion-confirmation prompts so the agent keeps checking an unfinished condition, consuming provider resources after the original task is done. The authors report testing Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks, with API requests amplified by up to 93.88 times while original task checks still pass.

entry.title: Adversarial Risk in the Generative AI Era: Why the Small Epsilon Ball Should Be Dropped
entry.summary: Adversarial Risk in the Generative AI Era Necessitates Dropping the Small Epsilon Ball arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper argues that adversarial machine learning research focuses too narrowly on epsilon-ball perturbations defined by ℓp norms, which give defenders a distorted view of risk. The authors contend this leads defenders to optimize narrow mathematical robustness at the expense of systemic security. They also argue it encourages attackers to exploit alternative adversarial pathways that do not overlap with the epsilon-ball threat model.

entry.title: ASCENT: Compiling exact norm constraints into compact lattice proofs
entry.summary: ASCENT: Algebraic Structured Compilation of Exact Norms for Succinct Lattice Proofs IACR ePrint · Nov 10, 2026This paper addresses exact ℓ2 norm constraints in lattice cryptography, where a witness must satisfy both modular equations and a shortness bound. It presents a reduction-of-knowledge compiler that turns the norm language for a committed lattice witness into a narrow structured relation made of commitment-opening constraints, tensor-structured inner-product claims, and relaxed admissible shortness bounds. The compiler adds O(1) prover-to-verifier communication independent of witness length and requires O(log N) verifier work, and the techniques can extend to folding for R1CS-type circuits. The authors estimate transcripts of about 27.69 KB for exact norm reduction and 27.75 KB for R1CS folding at 128-bit security, smaller than LatticeFold+ and SALSAA. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose compiling exact ℓ2-norm constraints into a structured algebraic relation with witness-length-independent communication, and report transcript sizes against LatticeFold+ and SALSAA.

entry.title: Homomorphism in Expectation: Homomorphic Encryption with Range-Relative Correctness
entry.summary: Homomorphism in Expectation: Leveled Homomorphic Encryption with Range-Relative Correctness IACR ePrint · Nov 10, 2026This paper introduces Homomorphism in Expectation (HIE), a construction showing that encrypted addition alone suffices for addition and multiplication in deep real-valued computation. Built from any additively homomorphic scheme over Z_2, it yields leveled homomorphic encryption for arithmetic circuits of arbitrary polynomial depth. New encoding and circuit evaluation techniques remove the exponential overhead of the direct bitstream approach. ★★★★ Notable: The authors build leveled homomorphic encryption for arbitrary polynomial depth using only additive encryption, removing exponential overhead, with explicit complexity bounds reported.

entry.title: New post-quantum PRFs and VRFs built from isogeny-based group actions
entry.summary: A New Class of PRFs and Efficient VRFs from Isogeny-based Group Actions IACR ePrint · Nov 10, 2026This paper shows that the security of Poly-style pseudorandom functions over composite-order class groups is governed by the smallest prime factor of the group order, not the largest as previously believed, and presents two generic attacks on this basis. The authors introduce a "restrict-then-expand" design paradigm and formalize multivariate polynomial PRFs (MP-PRFs) from group actions. They use this framework to construct new group-action-based verifiable random functions (VRFs) that require far fewer group-action evaluations than prior work at a near-128-bit proof-soundness level. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors show Poly-style PRF security is governed by the smallest prime factor of the group order and propose a restrict-then-expand paradigm, reporting attack complexity and VRF comparisons.

entry.title: Neural Cipher Bench: Measuring the Cost and Portability of Running Ciphers as Neural Networks
entry.summary: Neural Cipher Bench: Cost and Portability of Corner-ReLU Cipher Implementation IACR ePrint · Nov 10, 2026The paper implements AES, SM4, ARIA, Camellia, and ChaCha20 as bit-exact neural networks using one shared corner-ReLU construction, and derives a cost model for width, depth, and neuron count. Measurements on four platforms and five execution paths show that every configuration passing the correctness check ran slower than its classical baseline, with the best reaching 0.80×. Some AES configurations on the Apple Neural Engine produced incorrect outputs without any error, so mathematical bit-exactness does not guarantee backend bit-exactness and outputs from edge NPUs need validation.

entry.title: Attack on a Cayley-graph hash function: finding collisions faster than generic methods
entry.summary: Bounding the security of the Bromberg-Shpilrain-Vdovina hash function IACR ePrint · Nov 10, 2026This paper presents an attack that finds collisions in the Bromberg-Shpilrain-Vdovina hash functions, a family of Cayley hash functions with hashes given by matrices in SL_2(p) for a large prime p. Under an assumption similar to Zaremba's Conjecture on continued fractions, the attack has average-case time complexity O(p^0.28) for k=2 and O(p^0.36) for k=3. This improves on the general attacks of Mullan-Tsaban and Slaughter, which run in O(√p) on average. The authors also give examples of collisions found for large primes when k=2 and k=3.

entry.title: A tutorial on oblivious RAM, a method for hiding memory access patterns
entry.summary: A Tutorial on Oblivious Random Access Memory IACR ePrint · Nov 10, 2026This tutorial article gives an overview of Oblivious RAM (ORAM), a technique that protects memory access patterns in systems with untrusted memory. It reviews ORAM's security goals and threat models, describes the most popular constructions and their core mechanisms, and discusses practical implementation considerations. It aims to give readers a clear foundation for understanding ORAM-based memory protection and its applications.

entry.title: Recovering AES keys when only one bit leaks, using chosen plaintexts
entry.summary: When One Bit Is (Almost) Enough: A Low Leakage Chosen Plaintext Side Channel Attack on AES IACR ePrint · Nov 10, 2026This paper presents a new chosen plaintext strategy against AES that aims to recover the secret key even when side-channel leakage is very small. The authors use as an example a worst case in which only one bit position of the 128-bit SubBytes output leaks across rounds. The approach requires more traces than standard attacks because it relies on chosen plaintexts.

entry.title: Doubly-efficient private information retrieval built on modular forms
entry.summary: Doubly-Efficient Private Information Retrieval from Modular Forms IACR ePrint · Nov 9, 2026The paper presents information-theoretic protocols for multi-server private information retrieval in which each server stores only one extra bit beyond the database preprocessing structure, while query time stays sublinear. With two servers, server time is n^0.82, matching prior state-of-the-art, but storage drops from O(n√log n) bits to n+1 bits. The construction relies on Fourier-sparse cone-delta functions, which are built using modular forms and the valence formula. ★★★★ Notable: The authors build Fourier-sparse cone-delta functions via modular forms and the valence formula, generalizing matching-vector methods to give doubly-efficient PIR with n+1 bits storage and improved se

entry.title: SEC: A Secret Sharing Scheme Giving Each Party One Short Share
entry.summary: SEC: One-Share Everywhere-Short Secret Sharing from Lossless Expanders IACR ePrint · Nov 9, 2026This paper introduces SEC, an expander-code-based ramp secret sharing scheme over Z-modules aimed at lattice-based distributed cryptography. Each participant receives exactly one share regardless of the number of parties or thresholds, and bounded secret coefficients yield bounded share coefficients and reconstruction vectors. The authors prove correctness, everywhere-shortness, and linearity, and introduce hard-core local leakage resilience, proven secure under the MatrixHint-MLWE problem. ★★★★ Notable: The authors build a one-share everywhere-short secret sharing scheme from lossless expanders, with proofs of correctness and a leakage-resilience analysis under MLWE-based assumptions.

entry.title: Paper "On Composing Oracle Separations": how black-box separation results combine
entry.summary: On Composing Oracle Separations IACR ePrint · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies how black-box separations, which show that certain primitives cannot be built from specific building blocks, combine when several blocks are used together. The authors propose technical conditions under which two black-box separations compose, so the target primitive is also separated from black-box combinations of both blocks. The main application shows that combining indistinguishability obfuscation (iO) with collision-resistant hash functions is unlikely to yield hard problems in SZK, and so is unlikely to suffice for lossy functions or fully homomorphic encryption. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose conditions under which black-box separations compose, extending iO lower bounds from one-way permutations to combinations with collision-resistant hashing.

entry.title: The isodual constant of the LLL potential: exact values and structure
entry.summary: The isodual constant of the LLL potential: exact values and structure IACR ePrint · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies an isodual lattice invariant η(L), defined by minimizing the LLL potential over lattice bases and normalizing by the determinant. The authors prove that its maximum in dimension 5 is η_5=6, attained only by D_5 and its dual, with computer-assisted verification. They also prove η_8=2304, attained by E_8, and show that μ_m equals Hermite's constant γ_m for m≤5. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report exact values η5=6 and η8=2304 and bound the Ψ-Hermite constant μm, a new result on lattice invariants; code and data are public, though proofs are computer-assisted.

entry.title: γ₁₁: Reduction by Sections for Two Macadamia Cases
entry.summary: γ₁₁: Reduction by Sections — the macadamias 0019 and 0017 IACR ePrint · Nov 9, 2026This paper continues a series on the Hermite constant in dimension 11, whose value is given as γ₁₁=4/¹¹√972. It studies chains of lattices of ranks 11, 10 and 9, where the rank-9 lattice lies over one of 4,487,813 perfect forms. The authors settle two of the ten remaining cases, called macadamias, namely 0019:030884313 and 0017:001746552. They prove that every admissible chain whose rank-9 member is marked by these forms has determinant at least 972. The method is reduction by sections, and the finite checks are computer-assisted.

entry.title: γ₁₁: One Selected Contact, Two Linked Blocks — the macadamia 0030
entry.summary: γ₁₁: One Selected Contact, Two Linked Blocks — the macadamia 0030 IACR ePrint · Nov 9, 2026This paper is one of five companion papers completing the proof of γ₁₁=4/∜972 announced in a root paper and collected in "A Focus on Hermite Constant 11". It treats the rank-9 form 0030:030301719 of Λ₉ under Λ₁₀, selecting one contact of the reference lattice and applying a determinant–trace theorem to two eight-dimensional blocks sharing an off-diagonal column. The proof closes with a rational cover of three scalar parameters and is computer-assisted, with every leaf checked in exact rational arithmetic.

entry.title: γ₁₁: Unequal Triangles and Adapted References — the macadamia 0050
entry.summary: γ₁₁: Unequal Triangles and Adapted References — the macadamia 0050 IACR ePrint · Nov 9, 2026This paper is the ninth in a series on the Hermite constant in dimension 11, studying the perfect form P = 0050:024468269 of rank 9 with determinant 8192/9 and minimum 4. The authors prove that every admissible lattice chain whose rank-9 member is admissibly marked by P has determinant at least 972. The proof is computer-assisted with explicit finite checks, and reduces the problem to a five-parameter root case.

entry.title: Twisted Towers: A Faster, Fully Costed SexTNFS Attack on BLS12-381
entry.summary: Twisted Towers: A Faster and Fully Costed SexTNFS Attack IACR ePrint · Nov 9, 2026This paper studies a special exTNFS attack on discrete logarithms in the target group of BLS12-381. It presents a (6,2) design whose every step, from relation collection to individual logarithms, is priced in one instruction-level model. The design uses an explicit twisted tower so that relations and ideals come in orbits of four. The authors also note that yield estimates over TNFS coefficient cubes overcount unit multiples. All estimates rest on stated heuristics, nothing was run at full size, and BLS12-381's practical security is unchanged.

entry.title: A paper proposing a flexible cryptographic scheme combining homomorphic encryption and post-quantum key encapsulation for private health data.
entry.summary: An Agile Homomorphic Encryption and ML-KEM Scheme for Privacy-Preserving Health Data Processing IACR ePrint · Nov 9, 2026This paper proposes an agile cryptographic scheme that combines ML-KEM and the BGV homomorphic encryption scheme. It is designed to allow efficient implementation in an embedded use case, with health data processing as the motivating application. The authors describe the parameter selection for the scheme and demonstrate its feasibility with a proof-of-concept implementation.

entry.title: Closest Vector Problem on Gadget Lattices: Algorithms and Geometry
entry.summary: The Closest Vector Problem on Gadget Lattices: Efficient Algorithms and Voronoi Geometry IACR ePrint · Nov 9, 2026This paper studies the Closest Vector Problem (CVP) on gadget lattices, which are widely used in lattice-based cryptography and error-correcting codes. The authors give efficient exact CVP algorithms for power and CRT gadget lattices and their duals, including a deterministic linear-time solver for the parity-check power gadget lattice. They also analyze existing decoders and examine the Voronoi cell geometry of these lattices.

entry.title: Multi-Hop Functional Encryption: a new cryptographic primitive for controlled release of intermediate results
entry.summary: Multi-Hop Functional Encryption IACR ePrint · Nov 9, 2026This paper introduces multi-hop functional encryption (MHFE), a new primitive for computing over encrypted data in recursive, multi-stage workflows. Each node in a directed-acyclic computation graph holds a restricted key that reveals only that node's output, while computation continues downstream on a forwardable encrypted state.
